meta.desc: The Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebidu (12th century) is anarchitectural marvel of Hoysala architecture, built in chloritic schist with a stellate (star-shaped) plan that maximizes sculptural surfaces. It features a sanctum, vestibule, and mandapa with lathe-turned pillars, intricately carved ceilings, and exterior walls covered in deep-relief panels depicting deities and epics.

meta.desc: Hoysaleshwara temple, also referred simply as the Halebidu temple, is a 12th-century Hindu temple dedicated to the god Shiva. It is the largest monument in Halebidu, a town in the state of Karnataka, India and the former capital of the Hoysala Empire. The temple was sponsored by King Vishnuvardhana of the Hoysala Empire. Its construction started around 1121 CE and was complete in 1160 CE.

meta.title: File:The mantapa of the Hoysaleswara Temple.jpg
meta.desc: The mantapa of the Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebidu is a large, open pillared hall that serves as the main congregational space for devotees. It is supported by lathe-turned pillars, a hallmark of Hoysala craftsmanship, which are polished, symmetrical, and precisely shaped using a lathe technique to create uniform cylindrical forms with intricate fluting and decorative motifs.

meta.title: File:Shiva and Parvati relief at Hoysaleswara temple.jpg
meta.desc: The Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebidu (12th century) is anarchitectural marvel of Hoysala architecture, built in chloritic schist with a stellate (star-shaped) plan that maximizes sculptural surfaces. It features a sanctum, vestibule, and mandapa with lathe-turned pillars, intricately carved ceilings, and exterior walls covered in deep-relief panels depicting deities and epics.

meta.title: File:Lathe-Turned Pillar at Hoysaleshwara Temple, Halebidu, Karnataka.jpg
meta.desc: A richly finished lathe-turned stone pillar inside the Hoysaleshwara Temple at Halebidu, a 12th-century Hoysala monument dedicated to Shiva. The temple is renowned for its finely carved soapstone architecture and sculptural detailing. This photograph highlights the polished circular mouldings of the pillar, adjoining carved supports and the stone railing overlooking the temple grounds.

The closely spaced columns create a rhythmic arrangement throughout the mandapa.
